steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on meta-learning structured prompts with a new soft verbalizer for few-shot text classification with masked language models. Motivate prompt learning and prompt tuning, explain the problems with MetaPrompting, describe our method (MetaPrompter and RepVerb), and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Large pre-trained LMs; cost of fine-tuning; parameter-efficient alternatives
- Prompt learning with discrete prompts and verbalizers
- Prompt tuning with continuous prompts
- Initialization sensitivity and the problems of MetaPrompting
- Our approach: meta-learned prompt pool with attention
- RepVerb, a representative verbalizer
- MetaPrompter, experiments, contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - fine-tuning whole model (cite) effective, widely used, but optimizing + storing task-specific params compute- and memory-expensive for large models (e.g. GPT-3 (cite), 100+ billion parameters)
  - alternatives: adapter tuning (cite), prompt learning (cite)
  - prompt learning preferable: effective, plugs into pre-trained MLM without invasive modification (cite)
- Prompt learning
  - downstream task as cloze-style MLM problem
  - good for few-shot: effective, parameter-efficient, plug-and-play (cite)
  - wrap input with discrete prompt (e.g. “ Topic is [MASK] ”), MLM predicts token at [MASK]
  - verbalizer (cite) maps predicted token to label
  - designing an effective prompt needs good understanding of downstream tasks
- Prompt tuning
  - wrap input embedding with continuous prompt (cite)
  - MLM frozen to reduce parameters learned
  - continuous prompt + discrete tokens -> template (cite)
- Initialization + MetaPrompting
  - prompt tuning sensitive to initialization (cite); approaches to alleviate it (cite)
  - MetaPrompting (cite): state-of-the-art, meta-learning (cite) a meta-initialization for all task-specific prompts
  - problem 1: complex tasks -> hard to get good prompts for all tasks/samples from one meta-initialized prompt
  - problem 2: hand-crafted verbalizer; choosing label tokens labor-intensive, not scalable for large label set
  - problem 3: expensive tuning of whole MLM; Figure 1: large gap in meta-testing accuracy with/without MLM tuning (details Section 4)
- Our approach
  - pool of multiple prompts (cite) to extract task knowledge from meta-training tasks
  - instance-dependent prompts = weighted combinations of pool prompts via attention (cite); query = instance's feature embedding
  - prompt pool = shared meta-knowledge, learned by MAML algorithm (cite)
  - base learner: meta-parameter + support set -> task-specific prompt pool; meta-learner optimizes meta-parameter on query set
  - more flexible than single prompt initialization (MetaPrompting), better for complex tasks
  - only prompt pool tuned -> much more parameter-efficient (1000\times fewer parameters)
- RepVerb
  - novel soft verbalizer: label embeddings = average feature embeddings of corresponding training samples
  - no human effort for label token selection
  - no extra parameters; Section 4.2: more effective than soft verbalizers in WARP (cite), DART (cite), ProtoVerb (cite)
  - learned feature embedding more discriminative

  - six widely used classification data sets
  - RepVerb beats existing soft verbalizers, also helps other prompt-based methods like MetaPrompting
  - MetaPrompter better than recent state-of-the-arts

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, large pre-trained language models have been very successful in solving many different downstream tasks. Fine-tuning the whole model works well and is widely used, but when the model is large, optimizing and storing all the task-specific parameters can be expensive in compute and memory (for example, GPT-3 has 100+ billion parameters). Many approaches were proposed to deal with this issue, for example adapter tuning and prompt learning. Prompt learning is more preferable though, because it is effective and also because it can be easily plugged into a pre-trained MLM without invasive modification.

Prompt learning formulates the downstream task as a cloze-style MLM problem. It is useful for few-shot tasks because it is effective, parameter-efficient, and plug-and-play. In prompt learning, an input text is wrapped with a discrete prompt (e.g., “ Topic is [MASK] ”) and given to the MLM, which predicts a token at the [MASK] position. Then a verbalizer maps the predicted token to the label. But to design an effective prompt you need a good understanding of the downstream tasks.

More recently, prompt tuning proposes to wrap the input embedding with a continuous prompt instead. The MLM is kept frozen so that fewer parameters need to be learned. The continuous prompt can also be combined with discrete tokens to form a template.

Prompt tuning can be sensitive to initialization, and a number of approaches were recently proposed to alleviate this. In particular, MetaPrompting is the state-of-the-art method, and it uses meta-learning to learn a meta-initialization for all the task-specific prompts. However, MetaPrompting has three problems. 1. When the tasks are complex, it is hard to get good prompts for all tasks and samples starting from a single meta-initialized prompt. 2. MetaPrompting uses a hand-crafted verbalizer, and choosing good label tokens for a hand-crafted verbalizer is labor-intensive and does not scale to a large label set. 3. MetaPrompting needs expensive tuning of the whole MLM. In Figure 1 there is a large gap between the meta-testing accuracies with and without MLM tuning (the experimental details are in Section 4).

- Our approach
  - pool of multiple prompts (cite) to extract task knowledge from meta-training tasks
  - instance-dependent prompts = weighted combinations of pool prompts via attention (cite); query = instance's feature embedding
  - prompt pool = shared meta-knowledge, learned by MAML algorithm (cite)
  - base learner: meta-parameter + support set -> task-specific prompt pool; meta-learner optimizes meta-parameter on query set
  - more flexible than single prompt initialization (MetaPrompting), better for complex tasks
  - only prompt pool tuned -> much more parameter-efficient (1000\times fewer parameters)

- RepVerb
  - novel soft verbalizer: label embeddings = average feature embeddings of corresponding training samples
  - no human effort for label token selection
  - no extra parameters; Section 4.2: more effective than soft verbalizers in WARP (cite), DART (cite), ProtoVerb (cite)
  - learned feature embedding more discriminative

- MetaPrompter + results + contributions
  - meta-learning structured prompts + RepVerb = MetaPrompter
  - six widely used classification data sets
  - RepVerb beats existing soft verbalizers, also helps other prompt-based methods like MetaPrompting
  - MetaPrompter better than recent state-of-the-arts

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the last few years, large pre-trained language models have been very successful in solving many different downstream tasks. Fine-tuning the whole model works well and is widely used, but when the model is large, optimizing and storing all the task-specific parameters can be expensive in compute and memory (for example, GPT-3 has 100+ billion parameters). Many approaches were proposed to deal with this issue, for example adapter tuning and prompt learning. Prompt learning is more preferable though, because it is effective and also because it can be easily plugged into a pre-trained MLM without invasive modification.

Prompt learning formulates the downstream task as a cloze-style MLM problem. It is useful for few-shot tasks because it is effective, parameter-efficient, and plug-and-play. In prompt learning, an input text is wrapped with a discrete prompt (e.g., “ Topic is [MASK] ”) and given to the MLM, which predicts a token at the [MASK] position. Then a verbalizer maps the predicted token to the label. But to design an effective prompt you need a good understanding of the downstream tasks.

More recently, prompt tuning proposes to wrap the input embedding with a continuous prompt instead. The MLM is kept frozen so that fewer parameters need to be learned. The continuous prompt can also be combined with discrete tokens to form a template.

Prompt tuning can be sensitive to initialization, and a number of approaches were recently proposed to alleviate this. In particular, MetaPrompting is the state-of-the-art method, and it uses meta-learning to learn a meta-initialization for all the task-specific prompts. However, MetaPrompting has three problems. 1. When the tasks are complex, it is hard to get good prompts for all tasks and samples starting from a single meta-initialized prompt. 2. MetaPrompting uses a hand-crafted verbalizer, and choosing good label tokens for a hand-crafted verbalizer is labor-intensive and does not scale to a large label set. 3. MetaPrompting needs expensive tuning of the whole MLM. In Figure 1 there is a large gap between the meta-testing accuracies with and without MLM tuning (the experimental details are in Section 4).

In this paper we use a pool of multiple prompts to extract task knowledge from the meta-training tasks. Then we build instance-dependent prompts as weighted combinations of all the prompts in the pool, using attention. The query vector of the attention is the feature embedding of the instance. The prompt pool is the shared meta-knowledge and it is learned with the MAML algorithm. Given a task with a support set and a query set, the base learner uses the meta-parameter and the support set to build a task-specific prompt pool, and then the meta-learner optimizes the meta-parameter on the query set. Meta-learning a prompt pool is more flexible than meta-learning just a single prompt initialization like MetaPrompting does, and it adapts better to complex tasks. Also, since only the prompt pool is tuned, it is much more parameter-efficient than MetaPrompting (it has 1000\times fewer parameters).

We also propose a new soft verbalizer, the representative verbalizer (RepVerb). RepVerb builds label embeddings by averaging the feature embeddings of the training samples of each label. Unlike manually-designed verbalizers, it needs no human effort to select label tokens. Also, RepVerb does not need to learn any additional parameters, and the empirical results in Section 4.2 show that it is more effective than the soft verbalizers in WARP, DART, and ProtoVerb. In addition the feature embedding learned by RepVerb is more discriminative.

We call the whole procedure, which combines meta-learning the structured prompts with RepVerb, MetaPrompter. We run experiments on six widely used classification data sets. The results show that RepVerb is better than existing soft verbalizers, and that it also helps other prompt-based methods like MetaPrompting. MetaPrompter also performs better than the recent state-of-the-arts.

Our contributions are: 1. We propose MetaPrompter, a parameter-efficient algorithm for effective structured prompting. 2. We propose RepVerb, a simple and effective soft verbalizer. 3. Experimental results show that MetaPrompter is effective and parameter-efficient.

Many approaches have been proposed to alleviate this issue, such as adapter tuning [11,12,13] and prompt learning [14,15,8,9,16,17,18,19,20]. Prompt learning formulates the downstream task as a cloze-style MLM problem, and is useful for few-shot tasks due to its effectiveness, parameter-efficiency, and plug-and-play nature [14,8,20]. Specifically, it wraps an input text with a discrete prompt (e.g., “ Topic is [MASK] ”) and feeds it to the MLM to predict a token at the [MASK] position. A verbalizer [9,24,25] then maps the predicted token to the label. However, designing an effective prompt requires a good understanding of the downstream tasks.

Recently, prompt tuning [9,16,26] proposes to wrap the input embedding with a continuous prompt, keeping the MLM frozen to reduce the number of parameters to be learned. The continuous prompt can further be combined with discrete tokens to form a template [16,27,24].

Prompt tuning can be sensitive to initialization [9], and a number of approaches have recently been proposed to alleviate this problem [9,28,29]. In particular, MetaPrompting [30] is the state-of-the-art, using meta-learning [31,32,33] to learn a meta-initialization for all task-specific prompts. However, MetaPrompting suffers from three problems. 1. When the tasks are complex, it is challenging to obtain good prompts for all tasks and samples from a single meta-initialized prompt. 2. In this paper, we use a pool of multiple prompts [28,34,35] to extract task knowledge from meta-training tasks, and then construct instance-dependent prompts as weighted combinations of all the prompts in the pool via attention [36], whose query vector is the instance's feature embedding. The prompt pool is the shared meta-knowledge and is learned by the MAML algorithm [33]. Specifically, given a task with a support set and a query set, the base learner takes the meta-parameter and the support set to build a task-specific prompt pool, and the meta-learner then optimizes the meta-parameter on the query set. Meta-learning a prompt pool is more flexible than meta-learning only a single prompt initialization (as in MetaPrompting), and allows better adaptation to complex tasks. Moreover, since only the prompt pool is tuned, it is much more parameter-efficient than MetaPrompting (with 1000\times fewer parameters).

We also propose a novel soft verbalizer, the representative verbalizer (RepVerb), which constructs label embeddings by averaging the feature embeddings of the corresponding training samples. Unlike manually-designed verbalizers, RepVerb requires no human effort for label token selection. Moreover, RepVerb does not require learning any additional parameters, and empirical results in Section 4.2 demonstrate that it is more effective than the soft verbalizers in WARP [21], DART [26], ProtoVerb [10]. Besides, the feature embedding learned by RepVerb is more discriminative.

The whole procedure, combining meta-learning the structured prompts and RepVerb, is called MetaPrompter in the sequel. Experiments on six widely used classification data sets demonstrate that RepVerb outperforms existing soft verbalizers and also benefits other prompt-based methods such as MetaPrompting. Moreover, MetaPrompter achieves better performance than the recent state-of-the-arts.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: 1. We propose MetaPrompter, a parameter-efficient algorithm for effective structured prompting. 2. We propose a simple and effective soft verbalizer (RepVerb). 3. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and parameter-efficiency of MetaPrompter.
